title: International Scholarships for Indonesian Students: Full Guide
summary: Discover the best international scholarships for Indonesian students, how to apply, what to prepare, and tips to boost your chances of winning funding abroad.

[Living Abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/living-abroad/)


Let’s be honest: the dream of studying abroad feels incredible until you open a university fee page and your heart sinks a little. Tuition, living costs, flights, it adds up fast. But here’s the thing: thousands of Indonesian students land full funding every single year through **international scholarships** , and most of them started exactly where you are right now. Curious, slightly overwhelmed, and Googling their way to answers.


If you’ve ever wondered whether scholarships abroad are actually within reach for someone like you, the short answer is yes. This guide will walk you through everything a beginner needs to know, from understanding the types of international scholarships for Indonesian students to building an application that actually gets noticed. If you’re also figuring out the bigger picture of going abroad, check out[How to Study Abroad from Indonesia: A Complete Guide](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-study-abroad-from-indonesia/) for a solid foundation.

##


**What Are International Scholarships and Who Are They For?**


International scholarships are funding programs offered by governments, universities, private foundations, and international organizations to support students who want to study outside their home country. Some cover everything, tuition, flights, monthly living allowance, health insurance. Others are partial, covering just a portion of your costs.


The good news? Many of these programs actively recruit students from Indonesia. The country is large, diverse, and produces high-achieving graduates that scholarship committees genuinely want in their programs.


###


**1. Government-Funded Scholarships**


These are offered by a foreign government to attract talented international students. Popular examples include the Chevening Scholarship (UK), the DAAD (Germany), the Fulbright Program (USA), the Australia Awards, the Dutch Government Scholarship (NFP), and the Japanese Government Scholarship (MEXT). They tend to be highly competitive but also among the most generous.


###


**2. University Scholarships**


Many top universities offer their own merit-based or need-based grants for international applicants. These can range from partial tuition waivers to fully funded packages. You often apply for these at the same time as your university admission.


###


**3. Indonesian Government Scholarships for Abroad**


LPDP (Lembaga Pengelola Dana Pendidikan) is Indonesia’s flagship scholarship for studying overseas. It funds master’s and doctoral degrees at top global universities and is open to Indonesian citizens who meet the eligibility criteria. This is one of the most accessible entry points for Indonesian students specifically.


###


**4. Private and Foundation Scholarships**


Organizations like the Ford Foundation, Rotary Foundation, and various corporate sponsors offer scholarships with specific focus areas, leadership, social impact, STEM, arts, and more. These are worth hunting for if you have a niche strength or passion.


##


**Key Requirements You Need to Know**


Every scholarship has its own criteria, but there are common requirements that appear almost universally. Getting these right early gives you a massive head start.


###


**1. Academic Transcripts and GPA**


Most international scholarships for Indonesian students expect a strong academic record. A GPA of 3.0 out of 4.0 is often the minimum, but highly competitive programs expect closer to 3.5 or above.


###


**2. English Proficiency Test Scores**


You’ll need either an *IELTS* or *TOEFL iBT* score for most English-speaking countries. Some programs also accept *Duolingo English Test* now. Start preparing early, these tests take time and money to sit.


###


**3. Letters of Recommendation**


Usually two to three letters from professors, employers, or mentors who can speak to your academic ability, character, and potential. Choose recommenders who know you well, not just those with impressive titles.


###


**4. Statement of Purpose or Personal Essay**


This is your chance to tell your story. Why do you want to study this program? Why this country? How does it connect to your future plans? A genuine, specific, well-structured essay wins over a generic one every time.


###


**5. Research Proposal (for Postgraduate Applicants)**


If you’re applying for a master’s by research or a PhD, most programs require a research proposal. This needs to show that your topic is relevant, original, and feasible within the scope of the program.


##


**How to Find the Right Scholarship for You**


With hundreds of options out there, the trick is not to chase everything. Focus on the scholarships that align with your field, your level of study, and your destination. Here’s how to narrow it down smartly.


###


**1. Start With Your Destination Country**


Your target country shapes everything. Thinking about Japan? MEXT is your starting point. Interested in Singapore? Look into the ASEAN scholarships and university-specific grants. Curious about why so many Indonesians choose certain destinations?[this article on why Indonesians move abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/why-do-many-indonesians-work-abroad/) gives some interesting context on the broader pattern.


###


**2. Match the Scholarship to Your Study Level**


Some scholarships are undergraduate-only. Others focus on master’s or PhD students. LPDP, Chevening, and DAAD, for instance, are postgraduate programs. Make sure you’re applying for something you’re actually eligible for.


###


**3. Look at Field-Specific Programs**


If you’re in engineering, public health, or education, there are scholarships specifically designed for those fields. Narrowing by subject can actually increase your odds because the pool is smaller and the committee understands your background better.


###


**4. Use Reputable Scholarship Databases**


Websites like Scholars4Dev, DAAD Scholarship Database, and university official pages are reliable sources. Be cautious of third-party sites that ask for money upfront, legitimate scholarships never charge application fees.


##


**Tips to Strengthen Your Application**


A strong application is built over months, not days. Here are practical moves that make a real difference.


- **Start at least 12 months before the deadline.** Most scholarship cycles open once a year, and preparation takes longer than you think.
- **Tailor every application.** Copy-paste essays are easy to spot. Show the committee that you understand their program specifically.
- **Build relevant experience.** Volunteering, research assistantships, internships, and community projects all strengthen your profile.
- **Get feedback on your essays.** Ask a trusted mentor, a lecturer, or even a study-abroad alumnus to review your writing before you submit.
- **Prepare for interviews early.** Many government scholarships include panel interviews. Practice out loud, not just in your head.
- **Apply to more than one.** Don’t put all your eggs in one basket. Apply to three to five scholarships simultaneously if timelines allow.


##


**What Happens After You Win a Scholarship?**


Winning is amazing, but there’s still work to do. You’ll need to accept your offer within a deadline, sort out your student visa, arrange accommodation, and manage your living budget once you arrive. If your scholarship includes a monthly stipend sent from abroad, you’ll also need a reliable way to receive or transfer money internationally. Using a trusted *remittance* service like Transfez can make managing cross-border transfers simpler and more transparent, whether you’re receiving funds from home or sending back savings.


Also, take time to connect with your scholarship community. Alumni networks are invaluable for navigating life abroad and opening doors after graduation.
